Masterpiece Cakeshop v. Colorado. In June 2018, the Supreme Court ruled seven to two that Colorado's civil rights agency violated the First Amendment by displaying hostility toward religion when it sanctioned a baker who refused to design a wedding cake for a same-sex couple. Justice Kennedy wrote the majority opinion, which narrowly decided the case without setting broad precedent for religious exemptions from public accommodation laws. The baker, Jack Phillips, had refused to create a custom cake for Craig and Mullins' same-sex wedding, invoking religious beliefs about marriage. Colorado's Civil Rights Commission had ordered him to make such cakes, but Kennedy's majority focused on the Commission's conduct during the proceedings. The majority found that the Commission had shown clear bias against his religious views, particularly citing a commissioner's statement that religious objections to same-sex marriage echoed pro-slavery and pro-segregation arguments. Kennedy's opinion expressly declined to resolve the broader question of whether a business can refuse services based on religious objections. He also did not address whether the state's public accommodation law was constitutional as applied. The two dissenters, Justices Ginsburg and Sotomayor, argued the case was straightforward application of public accommodation laws to prevent discrimination. The decision ultimately set up later test cases like 303 Creative v. Elenis to directly address religious exemptions.
